activities.caption: file each witness — primary, secondary or tertiary
activities.name: hhwSourcesBuckets

config.prompt: Three layers of sources — file each witness:

items.label: a soldier's letter from the Somme, written the week of the battle
a parliamentary transcript of a wartime debate
a manor's account roll, kept to collect revenue
a 1960s memoir about 1916 — read for what it says of 1916
a modern historian's statistical reconstruction of that economy
an encyclopedia compilation, fine for orientation

config.why: The labels are about role, not reliability: the tax roll was written to collect revenue, not to describe the economy, and the memoir is primary for 1960s memory while secondary for 1916. Reliability is judged source by source, never by type.

activities.caption: one building, four lives — line them up, earliest first
activities.name: hhwHagiaOrder

config.prompt: The Hagia Sophia's layers — order them, earliest first:
items: A church — gold mosaics and a vast dome declaring Justinian's power and his God's glory to a mostly illiterate world
A mosque — minarets rise and Arabic calligraphy is set beside the Greek mosaics after 1453
A museum — the building opened to visitors as a secular monument
A mosque again — the most recent layer of its reading
config.why: The building is a primary source throughout — but what it is evidence of depends entirely on which layer you are reading. Knowing the sequence is the difference between reading the building and merely looking at it.

activities.anchor: Before using any source, historians interrogate it
activities.caption: pair each question with what it asks
activities.name: hhwCritMatch

config.prompt: The critic's questions — pair each with what it asks:

pairs.right: is it genuine — do paper, ink, language and handwriting fit the claimed date?
who wrote it, and from what background?
for whom was it meant — public or private?

config.why: The Donation of Constantine was exposed as an eighth-century forgery partly by linguistic analysis — its Latin looked nothing like fourth-century usage. Every source is an artefact of an intention; asking why it exists converts a passive quotation into evidence.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — what each source tells the truth about
activities.name: hhwPurposeSpot

config.prompt: One line of this source-purpose briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: A royal proclamation tells you what the state wanted its subjects to believe.
A soldier's letter tells you what one literate man chose to tell his family.
A merchant's ledger tells you what someone counted carefully because money depended on it.
A source's purpose is a side detail once its facts are confirmed.
A plain photograph still involves choices of framing and timing.
config.correction: Purpose is the master question: every source is an artefact of an intention — asking why the source exists converts a passive quotation into evidence.
config.why: Propaganda posters are honest about being propaganda; the subtle cases matter more — the victory memoir that downplays failures, the court chronicle that flatters its patron.

activities.caption: a chronicle and a tax roll disagree — your move?
activities.name: hhwConflictBranch

config.root: Two sources conflict about the same battle: a court chronicle that flatters its patron, and a tax roll that never mentions the fighting at all. You are the historian — decide.

start.text: The chronicle claims a great victory; the tax rolls for the same years show herds and households thinning fast.

choices.label: Trust the chronicle — it is the eye-witness account
choices.feedback: The chronicle was written to flatter a patron; its victory may be real and still not be what it says it is.

choices.label: Corroborate — find a third, independent source
choices.feedback: One source is a claim; independent sources agreeing move it toward fact.

choices.label: Read the tax roll against its grain
choices.feedback: The rolls never name the peasants, yet in aggregate they reveal households, obligations and famine years.

chronicle.text: You have one vivid account, written to impress — and nothing to check it against.

choices.label: Go back and corroborate
choices.feedback: Single pieces of evidence are checked against each other before any conclusion is drawn.

corroborate.text: A third source — a merchant's letter — agrees the war was costly but calls the battle a draw.

choices.label: Weigh the agreement: the cost is near-fact, the verdict still contested
choices.feedback: Where sources conflict is often where the interesting history lives — whose account differs, and why?

choices.label: Side with the chronicle anyway
choices.feedback: Disagreement is a lead, not an obstacle — the conflict itself needs explaining.

grain.text: The roll shows tithes falling for three consecutive years after the 'victory'.

choices.label: Treat the silence as evidence
choices.feedback: The history of the ordinary must often be reconstructed from the records of the people who owned, governed and wrote about them — which is itself a fact about power.

choices.label: Dismiss the roll — it never mentions the battle
choices.feedback: A biased source can be perfect evidence — of the bias, or of things it never intended to give.

end.text: Your claim is now hedged, sourced and checkable — the reasoning exposed where others can challenge it.

config.why: The historian's craft is reasoning from fragments under real uncertainty: sources interrogated rather than trusted, single pieces checked against each other, conclusions drawn in the open.

activities.anchor: resisting it is both the field's original sin
activities.caption: bet before you read on — after this, therefore because of this?
activities.name: hhwTriggerPredict

config.q: Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in June 1914; the war began in July. Is 'earlier than' enough to claim 'because of'?
choices: Yes — the assassination caused the war; the dates prove it
No — post hoc ergo propter hoc is the field's original sin: a causal claim needs a mechanism, the preconditions that made a spark dangerous, and the contingency of decisions along the way
Yes, provided the assassination comes first in every textbook
config.why: Historians separate trigger, preconditions and contingency, and test the argument against counterfactuals — if the alliance system had not existed, would the Sarajevo shots still have produced a general European war?

activities.anchor: is never a complete judgement of a source
activities.caption: fill the blanks — two axes, one habit
activities.name: hhwAxesCloze

config.text: Reliability asks whether a source can be %%0%% about what it claims; utility asks how useful it is for %%1%% — which is why 'limited value' is never a complete judgement of a source.
config.hint: One axis is about belief; the other is judged per purpose — and it can change from question to question.

activities.caption: line up SIFT — the old loop, renamed
activities.name: hhwSiftOrder

config.prompt: SIFT — the fact-checker's renaming of the old loop. Order the moves:
items: Trace the claim to its original context
config.why: Source criticism and corroboration renamed for the internet age — including 'reading laterally': judging a website not by reading it harder, but by leaving it to see what other sources say about it.
